title: Voice AI basics and Programming Fundamentals
goal: Know what the basic parts of any software system do and how they talk to each other, then how a voice agent works end to end.

concepts.title: An app works like a restaurant
concepts.summary: Dining room = frontend, waiter = API, kitchen = backend, pantry = database.
body: The dining room is the frontend: what you see and click.
The waiter is the API: it carries your request to the kitchen and brings the answer back, and it only accepts orders that are on the menu.
The kitchen is the backend: it does the work and applies the rules.
The pantry is the database: where everything is stored.
You never walk into the kitchen, and the browser never touches the database directly. Everything goes through the waiter.

concepts.title: Frontend: what people see and touch
concepts.summary: Runs on the user's device, shows the data and takes input. Never holds keys, never keeps the data.
body: On the web it runs in a browser and is built with HTML, CSS and JavaScript, usually React. On mobile it is built with React Native, Flutter or the platform's own tools.
It runs on the user's device, so anyone can look inside. A key in frontend code is a key you've given away.
It doesn't keep the data. It asks the backend for it, through an API.
RevRag's SDKs plug into a client's frontend: React and Angular on the web, React Native, Flutter and Android on mobile. You'll integrate one in P4.

concepts.title: Backend: where the work happens
concepts.summary: Every request goes through four steps: is it allowed, is it valid, do the work, reply.
body: Code running on a server, a computer that's always on somewhere else. Requests come in through doors such as GET /calls.

Step 1, is it allowed: checks who's asking, usually with an API key. Step 2, is it valid: checks the request has everything it needs. Step 3, do the work: reads or writes the database, or calls another service like an LLM. Step 4, reply: a status code and data, usually JSON.
The backend keeps the secrets, in settings called environment variables.
A webhook receiver (P3) and a Lambda (P5) are both tiny backends.

concepts.title: Database: where the data lives
concepts.summary: Tables of rows and columns, spoken to in SQL. It remembers, and only the backend talks to it.
body: Each row is one record (one call), each column is one detail, and id is the row's unique number.
GET /calls becomes a read: SELECT caller, summary FROM calls;
POST /calls becomes a write: INSERT INTO calls (caller, summary) VALUES ('Asha', 'Wants a loan');
The backend can restart and the data stays. Postgres keeps tables (P1); DynamoDB in week 5 keeps items you look up by a key.

concepts.title: Anatomy of a request and its reply
concepts.summary: A request has a method, an address, headers and a body. A reply has a status code and usually a body.
body: Method: what you want to do. GET reads, POST adds.
Address: where to send it, the server and then the door, such as https://my-call-log.onrender.com/calls.
Headers: extra details, like Content-Type: application/json and your API key.
Body: the data, written as JSON.
The reply has a status code, such as 201 Created, and usually a body with the saved record and its new id.

concepts.title: GET vs POST, and what replies mean
concepts.summary: 2xx it worked, 4xx fix your request, 5xx it's the server's problem.
body: 200 OK: it worked, here's your data. 201 Created: the new thing was saved.
400 Bad Request: the request is wrong or incomplete. 401 Unauthorized: the API key is missing or wrong. 404 Not Found: wrong address.
500 Server Error: something broke on the server.
When a client says the webhook isn't working, the status code is the first thing you look at.

concepts.title: Three ways to send the same request
concepts.summary: Browser (GET only), Postman (a form) and curl (one shareable command).
body: A browser can only send GET: paste the address and press Enter.
Postman: fill in the method, address, headers and body, then press Send. Start with the RevRag Postman collection.
curl: one command in the terminal. -X is the method, -H a header and -d the body. Easy to paste to an engineer so they can run exactly what you ran.

concepts.title: What happens when you open your P1 page
concepts.summary: Browser loads React, React calls GET /calls, the backend runs SELECT, rows come back as JSON, the list appears.
body: 1. You open the page and the browser loads the React code from Vercel.
2. React asks the backend: GET /calls. The backend checks the request.
3. The backend asks the database: SELECT * FROM calls.
4. The database sends the rows back.
5. The backend replies 200 OK with the calls as JSON.
6. React draws one line per call.
When a client says something is broken, an FDE's job is to work out which of these steps failed.

concepts.title: Local vs deployed: where your code runs
concepts.summary: localhost is only you. Deploying puts your code on always-on hosts: Vercel, Render and Neon.
body: Local: http://localhost:8000. Only you can open it, and it stops when your laptop sleeps.
Deployed: your code goes to GitHub and a hosting service runs it. Vercel runs the React page, Render the Python API, Neon the Postgres database.
Keys travel separately: in .env on your laptop, pasted into the host's settings page online. Never in code.
Works locally but broken online? Check for a missing key or an address still pointing at localhost. Render's free plan sleeps, so the first request can take up to a minute.

concepts.title: Every reply goes ears → brain → mouth
concepts.summary: Speech-to-text, then the LLM, then text-to-speech, then the loop starts again.
body: The ears: speech-to-text (STT) turns the caller's voice into written text.
The brain: the LLM reads the text, follows its prompt and writes a reply.
The mouth: text-to-speech (TTS) turns the reply into a natural-sounding voice.
The reply plays back to the caller and the loop starts again. Every step takes time, and the delays add up.

concepts.title: Why speed matters: waiting vs streaming
concepts.summary: One step at a time adds up to ~1.9 s of silence. Streaming overlaps the steps so the first word comes at ~0.6 s.
body: One step at a time: STT 0.5 s + LLM 1.0 s + TTS 0.4 s, and the caller waits 1.9 s for the first word.
Streaming: the LLM writes word by word and TTS starts speaking before the reply is done, so the first word arrives at about 0.6 s.
About 0.4 to 0.8 s feels natural. Past 1 to 2 s, callers talk over the agent.
Timings are illustrative.

concepts.title: Turn-taking: has the caller finished?
concepts.summary: A silence timer decides when it's the agent's turn. Too short cuts people off; too long feels slow.
body: People pause mid-sentence all the time, so the agent has to guess when they've finished.
Timer too short: the agent jumps in during a natural pause and cuts the caller off.
Timer too long: every reply starts late and the agent feels slow and robotic.
Smart turn detection also reads the words: "for my…" isn't finished yet. In RevRag this lives in the Speech tab: turn detection and response eagerness.

concepts.title: Interruptions: when the caller cuts in
concepts.summary: Barge-in means the agent stops the moment the caller talks. Noise and echo cause false alarms.
body: Barge-in: the agent stops the moment the caller starts talking, then listens. In RevRag: the interruption settings.
False alarms: a cough, a TV or street noise can look like an interruption. In RevRag: background noise.
Echo: the agent's own voice leaking back into the mic can sound like the caller cutting in.
Many complaints about agents that keep stopping or won't stop talking come down to these settings.

concepts.title: Where LiveKit fits
concepts.summary: A LiveKit room is like a Zoom call. Your agent is a program that joins it and runs STT → LLM → TTS.
body: You join the room from a browser (P2), or a phone call is connected into it through SIP (week 3).
Your agent program, Python from the quickstart, joins the same room as another participant.
It listens, sends the audio through STT, the LLM and TTS (AI services reached over the internet) and speaks back into the room.

concepts.title: The RevRag agent settings, placed on the call
concepts.summary: For each setting, ask which step of the call it changes: before, hear, think, speak or after.
body: Before the call: Pre-call processing gets things ready, like the lead's details.
Hear: the Speech tab, with the STT model, turn detection, interruption, response eagerness and background noise.
Think: the LLM model, the knowledge base and functions: which model thinks, what it knows and the actions it can take.
Speak: Voice and Pronunciation, how it sounds and how it says names and words.
After the call: Post-call processing, with summaries and outcomes sent on to the client's systems.
Across every step: Fallbacks, the backup plan for when something goes wrong.

concepts.title: Why P1 and P2? In week 3 they join up
concepts.summary: When a call with your bot ends, P2 sends a signed summary to P1. RevRag does the same for clients every day.
body: Your practice in week 3 (P3): when a call with your bot ends, the bot sends a summary to your app by webhook, signed with a shared secret.
Real client work: when a campaign call ends, RevRag sends the result to the client's CRM by webhook, signed and checked the same way.
Learn the pattern on your own projects first, then do it for real clients.

projects.title: A small call-log app
projects.summary: The restaurant from Part 1, built for real: Postgres on Neon, a Python API on Render, a React page on Vercel.
steps: Database: a Postgres table called calls, on Neon.
Backend: a Python API with GET /calls and POST /calls, on Render.
Frontend: a React page that lists the calls, on Vercel.
Push all the code to a GitHub repo in your own account, with a short README on how to run it.
projects.done_when: The page and the API run on public URLs, and a curl POST adds a row that shows up on the React page.

submit.label: The curl command you used to add a call
The Postman request you used to add a call

projects.warning: Keep the database's connection string private. It contains the password.

projects.title: Your own voice bot
projects.summary: The ears → brain → mouth loop, built with the LiveKit Voice AI quickstart and your own prompt.
steps: Create a free LiveKit Cloud account, then follow the Voice AI quickstart with Claude Code.
Give the bot a short prompt for a real use case, such as qualifying a loan lead.
Talk to it in the browser. Change one setting at a time (voice, turn detection, interruption) and note what each change does.
Push the code and your prompt to a GitHub repo in your own account.
projects.done_when: You can hold a 2-minute conversation with the bot, and you have notes on 3 setting changes.

submit.label: Link to a screen recording of a 2-minute conversation
Notes on 3 setting changes: what you changed, what you expected, what happened

projects.warning: Keep your LiveKit keys in .env and out of the repo.

quiz.question: In the restaurant analogy, which part of an app is the waiter?
quiz.explanation: The waiter carries your order to the kitchen and brings the dish back. That's the API, and it only accepts orders on the menu.

quiz.question: Why should the browser never talk to the database directly?
options: The frontend runs on the user's device, so any credentials in it would be exposed
Browsers are too slow for SQL
Databases only accept requests from Vercel
quiz.explanation: Anyone can look inside frontend code. Everything goes through the backend, which keeps the secrets.

quiz.question: A developer put an API key in their React code. What's the problem?
options: The key is visible to anyone who opens the page's code
quiz.explanation: The frontend runs on the user's device. A key in frontend code is a key you've given away.

quiz.question: Where do RevRag's SDKs plug in?
options: The client's frontend, web or mobile
quiz.explanation: A client's developer adds a few lines to their web or mobile app, and the voice agent appears inside it.

quiz.question: What is the first thing a backend checks on most requests?
options: Who's asking, usually with an API key
quiz.explanation: Step 1 is "is it allowed?". Then is it valid, do the work, and reply.

quiz.question: Where should a backend keep its database password?
options: In the code, as a constant
In environment variables, loaded from .env locally or the host's settings online
In the frontend, so it can pass it along
quiz.explanation: Secrets live in environment variables. Locally that's .env; on Render or Vercel you paste them into the settings page.

quiz.question: POST /calls usually becomes which SQL statement?
quiz.explanation: POST adds something new, which is an INSERT. GET /calls becomes a SELECT.

quiz.question: In the calls table, what does one row represent?
options: One detail, like the caller's name
quiz.explanation: Each row is one record, here one call. Each column is one detail about it.

quiz.question: Which part of a request carries the API key?
quiz.explanation: Headers carry extra details, like the format (Content-Type) and your API key.

quiz.question: What format is the request and reply body usually written in?
quiz.explanation: JSON: labels and values in curly brackets, readable by humans and machines.

quiz.question: A client's webhook call returns 401. Whose problem is it most likely?
options: The sender's: the API key is missing or wrong
quiz.explanation: 4xx means fix your request. 401 specifically means the key is missing or wrong.

quiz.question: You POST a new call and get back 201. What happened?
options: The request was missing a field
quiz.explanation: 201 Created: it worked and the new thing was saved.

quiz.question: Which status code means something broke on the server itself?
quiz.explanation: 5xx is the server's problem. 4xx is yours.

quiz.question: Why can't you add a call to P1 just by pasting the address into a browser?
options: A browser address bar only sends GET requests
You need to be logged in to Render
quiz.explanation: A browser can only read with GET. Use Postman or curl to send a POST.

quiz.question: In a curl command, what does -d set?
quiz.explanation: -X is the method, -H a header, -d the body.

quiz.question: In the P1 round trip, what happens right after React sends GET /calls?
options: The backend checks the request, then asks the database
quiz.explanation: The backend checks the request, then runs SELECT on the database, then replies with JSON.

quiz.question: Your P1 page works on your laptop but shows no calls on Vercel. What should you check first?
options: Whether the frontend still points at localhost, or a key is missing from the host's settings
quiz.explanation: The two most common causes are an address still pointing at localhost and a key missing from the host's settings.

quiz.question: The first request to your Render API after a break takes almost a minute. What's going on?
options: Render's free plan sleeps when idle and is waking up
quiz.explanation: That's normal on the free plan, not broken.

quiz.question: What is the correct order of the voice agent loop?
quiz.explanation: Ears (speech-to-text), then brain (LLM), then mouth (text-to-speech).

quiz.question: Why does streaming make a voice agent feel faster?
options: The steps overlap, so TTS starts speaking before the full reply is written
quiz.explanation: Each step works on partial results, so the first word arrives in well under a second instead of ~1.9 s.

quiz.question: Roughly how quickly should the first word of a reply arrive to feel natural?
options: It doesn't matter on a phone call
quiz.explanation: About 0.4 to 0.8 s feels natural. Past 1 to 2 s, callers start talking over the agent.

quiz.question: A client says their agent keeps cutting callers off mid-sentence. Which setting is the likeliest cause?
options: The turn-detection silence timer is too short
The knowledge base is too big
quiz.explanation: A timer that's too short makes the agent jump in during natural pauses. In RevRag it lives in the Speech tab.

quiz.question: The agent keeps stopping mid-sentence even though the caller is silent. Which of these could cause it?
options: The LLM prompt is too short
Background noise or echo being mistaken for the caller
The caller's phone is on Wi-Fi
quiz.explanation: Noise and echo cause false barge-ins. Check the background noise and interruption settings.

quiz.question: Sending a call summary to the client's CRM belongs to which settings area?
quiz.explanation: After the call: post-call processing sends summaries and outcomes on to the client's systems.

voice_quiz.prompt: Describe the ears, brain and mouth of a voice agent, and what each one does.
